conclusion.label: endorses

report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **well-supported by strong evidence**: exemestane does reduce breast cancer incidence in postmenopausal women at elevated risk, though the benefit must be weighed against modest harms and the population studied.

## Evidence

The key evidence comes from the **MAP.3 (NCIC CTG)** trial, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 study of 4,560 postmenopausal women with at least one risk factor for breast cancer (e.g., age ≥60, elevated Gail score, prior atypical hyperplasia or DCIS). Women received exemestane 25 mg/day or placebo for 5 years. At a median follow-up of 35 months, only 11 invasive breast cancers occurred in the exemestane group versus 32 in the placebo group — a statistically significant **65% relative risk reduction** in annual incidence of invasive breast cancer (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1103507; https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/research/exemestane-reduces-risk).

This finding has been independently corroborated across multiple secondary reports and reviews (https://www.onclive.com/view/exemestane-is-a-new-option-for-prevention-of-breast-cancer-in-postmenopausal-women; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3354700/), and the magnitude of effect (65% relative reduction) is consistently cited across independent sources, lending credibility.

**Caveats:** The absolute risk reduction was small (21 fewer cases in the exemestane arm over ~3 years among 2,285 women), reflecting the low absolute event rate even in "high-risk" populations. The USPSTF, reviewing exemestane alongside tamoxifen and raloxifene, found aromatase inhibitors carry "small to moderate harms" (bone loss, menopausal symptoms) and concluded that net benefit depends heavily on baseline risk — recommending against use in women not at increased risk (https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/breast-cancer-medications-for-risk-reduction).

**Bottom line:** The claim is accurate specifically for postmenopausal women at elevated risk; the trial evidence is robust, though benefits should be framed in absolute, not just relative, terms.
